title: “IF ANYONE COMES TO ME AND DOES NOT HATE HIS FATHER AND MOTHER…” — DID JESUS REALLY COMMAND HATRED?
paragraphs: “IF ANYONE COMES TO ME AND DOES NOT HATE HIS FATHER AND MOTHER…” — DID JESUS REALLY COMMAND HATRED?

One of Jesus’ hardest sayings sounds almost impossible to reconcile with the rest of Scripture—until you hear what He was actually demanding. And once you do, the disturbing word “hate” may expose something far closer to your heart than you expected.
There are verses people frame on walls.
Verses embroidered onto pillows.
Verses printed beneath sunsets and shared when life feels heavy.
Luke 14:26 is usually not one of them.
Jesus turns toward the crowds following Him and says:
“If anyone comes to me and does not hate his own father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, yes, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple.”
That is Luke 14:26.
Read it slowly.
Do not soften it yet.
Do not rush past the uncomfortable part.
Father.
Mother.
Wife.
Children.
Brothers.
Sisters.
Even your own life.
Then comes the word that makes modern readers recoil:
hate.
Did Jesus—the One who commanded us to love our enemies—actually command His disciples to hate their families?
Did the Christ who rebuked religious people for neglecting their parents suddenly tell people to despise their mothers and fathers?
Did the Savior who said, “Love one another,” somehow contradict Himself?
No.
But the truth is not that Jesus’ words were harmless.
The truth is that they were even more demanding than many of us realize.
And perhaps that is why this passage still makes us uncomfortable.
The Greek text of Luke 14:26 reads in part:
Εἴ τις ἔρχεται πρός με καὶ οὐ μισεῖ τὸν πατέρα ἑαυτοῦ καὶ τὴν μητέρα… οὐ δύναται εἶναί μου μαθητής.
The word translated “hate” is μισεῖ — misei, from μισέω — miseō.
It really is the ordinary Greek verb associated with hating.
We should not pretend the word means something completely different simply because Jesus’ sentence makes us uncomfortable.
But words live inside sentences.
Sentences live inside cultures.
And Scripture interprets Scripture.

Jesus was speaking within a Jewish, Semitic world in which stark contrasts could communicate preference, allegiance, or comparative love. The question therefore is not merely, “What can μισέω mean in a dictionary?” The question is, “What is Jesus communicating here, in this context, in harmony with His teaching elsewhere?”
Matthew gives us an enormously important parallel.
Jesus says:
“Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me, and whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me.”
That is Matthew 10:37.
There it is.
Not cruelty toward your mother.
Not contempt for your father.
Not abandonment of your children.
Not emotional hostility toward your spouse.
More than Me.
Luke gives us the shocking contrast.
Matthew makes the comparison explicit.
Jesus is demanding supreme allegiance.
Your love for Christ must stand so completely above every competing loyalty that, by comparison, no human relationship can be permitted to take His place.
And Scripture had already used similarly startling language.
In Genesis 29, Jacob loves Rachel more than Leah. The Hebrew text then describes Leah with the word שְׂנוּאָה — senu’ah, often rendered “hated.”
Yet the surrounding context shows the comparison: Rachel was loved more.
The language is intentionally sharp because the contrast is sharp.
Jesus uses language that stops the crowd in its tracks because He is not recruiting casual admirers.
He is calling disciples.
That distinction changes everything.
Imagine standing there.
You have heard about Him.
Perhaps you watched someone healed.
Perhaps you heard rumors about demons fleeing.
Perhaps you saw bread multiplied.
Perhaps everybody around you is talking about this Jesus of Nazareth.
The crowd is growing.
Excitement is spreading.
And Jesus does something strange.
He does not turn around and make discipleship easier to increase His numbers.
He makes the cost unmistakable.
Luke tells us that “great crowds” were traveling with Him.
Then Jesus turns toward them.
That detail matters.
He is essentially asking:
You are following Me now—but what happens when following Me costs you something?
What happens when your father does not understand?
What happens when your mother thinks you have gone too far?
What happens when friends mock your convictions?
What happens when obedience costs popularity?
What happens when your ambitions and Christ’s commands collide?
What happens when Jesus says one thing and the person whose approval you crave says another?
Who gets the final word?
That is where Luke 14 stops being an ancient theological puzzle.
Because suddenly the verse is standing inside your house.
Maybe you would never say that you love someone more than Jesus.
But whose disappointment controls you?
Whose approval can make you compromise?
Whose acceptance are you terrified of losing?
Whose voice becomes louder than Scripture when obedience becomes expensive?
Maybe the person competing with Christ is not your father or mother.
Maybe it is the person sleeping beside you.
Maybe it is the person you desperately want to marry.
Maybe it is your circle of friends.
Maybe it is your audience.
Maybe it is your career.
Maybe it is the version of yourself you have spent years constructing.
And then Jesus goes further.
“…yes, and even his own life…”
Now there is nowhere left to hide.
Because sometimes the greatest rival to Jesus is not another person.
It is me.
My comfort.
My plans.
My reputation.
My appetite.
My dreams.
My timetable.
My secret sin.
My right to decide what parts of my life Jesus may touch.
We can sing, “Jesus is Lord,” while quietly maintaining a list of exceptions.
Lord of Sunday.
Lord of worship music.
Lord of emergencies.
Lord when His will agrees with mine.
But not Lord of my sexuality.
Not Lord of my money.
Not Lord of my relationship.
Not Lord of my bitterness.
Not Lord of my career.
Not Lord of what I watch when nobody is looking.
Not Lord of the grudge I have justified for years.
Not Lord of the future I already planned without asking Him.
And Jesus refuses the arrangement.
He does not ask to become one important relationship among many.
He claims the throne.
That is why His next words are not sentimental:
“Whoever does not bear his own cross and come after me cannot be my disciple.”
Today, a cross can hang from a necklace.
To Jesus’ first hearers, a cross meant death.
Humiliation.
Execution.
There was nothing decorative about it.
Jesus was telling the crowd that discipleship meant surrender so deep that following Him could cost them everything.
And eventually, Jesus Himself would carry a cross.
This is where the scandal begins turning toward grace.
Because Christianity is not ultimately the story of human beings proving how much they can sacrifice for God.
It is first the story of what God has done for sinners who could never save themselves.
The One demanding everything from His disciples is the One who would give Himself for them.
Jesus did not merely teach about a cross.
He went to one.
He was betrayed.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Crucified.
And there, the sinless Son of God bore sin, giving Himself for sinners.
He died.
And He rose.
The Gospel is not “love Jesus enough and maybe He will accept you.”
The Gospel announces that salvation is by the grace of God, received through faith in Christ.
You do not purchase forgiveness by abandoning enough things.
You cannot bleed enough to erase your guilt.
You cannot perform enough religious acts to resurrect your own soul.
Christ saves.
Grace saves.
His blood—not your résumé—is the ground of forgiveness.
And yet the grace that saves us does not leave Jesus somewhere near the edge of our lives.
The Savior becomes Lord.
That is why biblical grace should never be confused with cheap permission to remain unchanged.
Jesus receives sinners.
Then Jesus transforms sinners.
He forgives.
He restores.
He teaches.
He disciplines.
He calls.
He changes what we love.
And sometimes that transformation creates painful moments when loyalty to Christ clashes with loyalty to people we deeply love.
But notice something crucial.
Supreme love for Christ does not authorize cruelty toward family.
Jesus affirmed the command to honor father and mother.
He condemned using religious excuses to avoid caring for parents in Mark 7.
Even while hanging on the cross, Jesus made provision for His mother, entrusting her to the beloved disciple in John 19:26–27.
Think about that.
The same Jesus who said that disciples must “hate” father and mother, in the comparative and allegiance-demanding sense of Luke 14, cared for His own mother while dying.
So if someone uses Luke 14:26 to justify abusing parents, despising a spouse, neglecting children, or behaving hatefully toward relatives, that person has missed Jesus’ meaning.
Christ is not commanding sinful hatred.
He is demanding unrivaled allegiance.
In fact, loving Jesus above your family should ultimately teach you how to love your family more faithfully.
You stop making people into gods.
You stop demanding that your spouse become your savior.
You stop making your children responsible for your identity.
You stop obeying parents when they demand what God forbids.
You stop worshiping human approval.
And because Christ occupies the place only Christ should occupy, you can love people as people rather than idols.
Sometimes loving Jesus first will make you more patient with your family.
Sometimes it will make you apologize.
Sometimes it will make you forgive.
Sometimes it will make you finally establish a righteous boundary.
Sometimes it will make you care for an aging parent when it is inconvenient.
Sometimes it will make you remain faithful when culture tells you faithfulness is foolish.
Sometimes it will make you tell someone you love:
“I love you deeply. But I cannot disobey Christ for you.”
And that sentence can hurt.
Because discipleship is beautiful.
But Jesus never advertised it as painless.
Perhaps that is why Luke 14:26 bothers us.
Maybe the deepest problem is not that we cannot understand the word “hate.”
Maybe we understand the demand behind it far too well.
Jesus will not share His throne.
And somewhere inside us, we know exactly which rival we do not want Him to touch.
So forget everyone else for a moment.
Forget the theological argument.
Forget the comment section.
Forget the person you wish would read this.
Ask yourself the question.
Who—or what—could make me walk away from Jesus?
A relationship?
Money?
Sex?
Success?
Family approval?
Fear of loneliness?
Political identity?
Social acceptance?
A hidden addiction?
Resentment toward God because He did not answer the prayer the way you wanted?
What would have to be threatened before you told Christ:
“You can have everything except that”?
Because whatever completes that sentence may reveal something you have placed dangerously close to His throne.
And perhaps this is where somebody reading needs to stop pretending.
You have been near Jesus without surrendering to Jesus.
Close enough to hear Christian language.
Close enough to share Christian posts.
Close enough to know the songs.
Close enough to look faithful.
But there is a locked room inside you.
And you know what is inside.
Jesus knows too.
Yet notice what He does with sinners who come to Him.
Peter denied Him.
Three times.
The disciple who swore he would never abandon Jesus collapsed under fear and insisted that he did not know Him.
What a scandal.
But Peter's failure was not the final chapter.
The risen Christ met him again.
Restored him.
Commissioned him.
Grace rewrote the story.
That does not mean Peter's denial did not matter.
Grace does not pretend sin is harmless.
Grace confronts sin, forgives the repentant sinner, and begins writing something new.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Maybe your scandal is not public.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe people think you are strong.
Maybe you have learned how to smile while your spiritual life quietly bleeds.
Maybe you love Jesus, but you are exhausted.
Maybe you have fallen again.
Maybe shame keeps whispering that after everything you have done, God must be finished with you.
Look at the cross.
The Gospel is not the announcement that good people finally managed to reach God.
It is the announcement that God came for sinners.
Repentance means we stop defending the darkness and turn toward Christ.
Faith means we stop trusting ourselves and entrust ourselves to Him.
Grace means forgiveness cannot be bought.
And discipleship means the Jesus who rescued us now has the right to lead us.
So no—Jesus was not commanding you to cultivate malicious hatred toward your mother, father, spouse, children, brothers, or sisters.
He was saying something that may be even harder:
Love Me above them all.
And above yourself.
Not because family is worthless.
Because Jesus is Lord.
Not because human love is evil.
Because even the best human love becomes destructive when asked to occupy God's throne.
Christ first.
Then let your love for everyone else flow from Him.
And if this exposed something hidden in you, do not perform for strangers.
Be honest before God.
Someone reading the comments may realize they are not the only believer still fighting.
And perhaps your honesty will become the reason another wounded Christian finally stops hiding.

And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you understand Scripture, follow and invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends who are willing to listen. Let them encounter daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and above all, the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
Jesus is not asking merely for your attention.
He is calling for you.
Your allegiance.
Your heart.
Your sin brought into the light.
Your idols removed from the throne.
Your life surrendered beneath His lordship.
The question is no longer, “Did Jesus really tell me to hate my family?”
The question underneath His shocking words is much more personal:
When every other love asks you to choose, will Jesus still be first?
Because one day you may discover that the hardest thing Christ asked you to surrender was the very thing keeping you from discovering how completely His grace could rewrite your story.
Some things Jesus asks you to release not because He wants your heart empty—but because His throne was never meant to be shared.
